chapters.title: One year of benefits
chapters.still: One year of benefit spending in Great Britain, £299 billion, shown as a pile of dots.

beats.narration: In 2024-25, people in Great Britain received £299 billion in benefits from the Department for Work and Pensions and Social Security Scotland.
That is in 2026-27 prices, to allow for inflation.
Scroll at any time to go at your own pace.

chapters.title: Your guess
chapters.still: A bar split into three parts: pensioners 51.5%, working-age and housing 33.6%, disability and carers 14.9%.

beats.narration: First, a question.
How do you think it splits between pensioners, disabled people and carers, and people of working age, including help with rent?
Drag the handles to make your guess. It stays on your device.
[calm, warm] Now it's your turn. Have a guess, then lock it in to carry on.

chapters.title: Benefit by benefit
chapters.still: The dots sorted into columns, one for each benefit. The State Pension is the largest.

beats.narration: Here is the same money, sorted by benefit.
The State Pension is the largest, at £138 billion.
Next, Personal Independence Payment and its Scottish version come to £30 billion. Universal Credit comes to £70 billion.
Benefits for pensioners make up 51.5% of the total, just over half.

chapters.title: Every constituency
chapters.still: A map of every constituency in Great Britain, coloured by benefit spending per resident.

beats.narration: Now each dot moves to the constituency where the person who received it lives.
There are 632 constituencies, each with its own MP. On this map, large rural areas take up the most space.
You can also show every constituency at the same size, which makes city areas easier to see.

chapters.title: Spending per person
chapters.still: Two 3D maps of the same constituencies. On one, height shows pensioner benefits per person aged 66 and over. On the other, height shows working-age benefits per person aged 16 to 64.

beats.narration: Now height shows spending per person, measured in two ways.
This one shows pensioner benefits for each person aged 66 and over.
This one shows working-age benefits for each person aged 16 to 64.
None of the 10 highest areas on one map is in the top 10 on the other.

chapters.title: North and south, or old and young
chapters.still: Each constituency as a dot, placed by the share of residents aged 66 and over and coloured by benefit spending per resident.

beats.narration: Here each constituency is a dot. Its colour shows benefit spending per resident.
Sorted from south to north, the colours are mixed. The link scores 0.24, where 1 would be a perfect match.
Sorted by the share of residents aged 66 and over, the link is stronger, at 0.44.
[calm, thoughtful] So spending per resident is linked more to age than to how far north an area is. That is why we compare each benefit with the age group it is for.

chapters.title: Your area
chapters.still: A box to enter your postcode, above the map of constituencies.

beats.narration: Each of these areas has its own page of figures.
[calm, warm] Enter your postcode to see how your area compares.
